The cases mark a new front in a season that has already stretched vector control teams across the region, with fogging trucks, aerial larviciding, and ground inspections underway to knock down mosquito populations before more people get sick. The confirmation, first reported by the Tampa Free Press, comes just days after neighboring Hillsborough County confirmed its own second locally acquired dengue case of the summer on August 5, following an initial case in late July, according to the Tampa Bay Times. That report noted the surge is tied to a dramatic jump in mosquito populations, with trap collections in Hillsborough County rocketing from 142 mosquitoes in a single trap in June to roughly 18,000 mosquitoes in mid-July following summer rainstorms. Hillsborough officials responded with multiple rounds of aerial and truck insecticide treatments, the newspaper reported. The Florida Department of Health in Pinellas County said it is coordinating dengue surveillance and prevention measures with Pinellas County Mosquito Control, which participates in the broader effort to track and contain the virus locally. In response to the new cases, vector control teams increased truck fogging, conducted aerial larviciding, and carried out targeted ground inspections to find and eliminate potential mosquito breeding sites. Warning Signs Came Before the Diagnoses Pinellas County Mosquito Control had already flagged rising risk days earlier. On August 7, the agency issued a public advisory warning that mosquito-borne virus transmission had increased locally following heavy summer rains, per Pinellas County Government. That warning arrived before the two human dengue cases were confirmed, underscoring how vector control officials detected the elevated threat ahead of the diagnoses. The timing fits a pattern playing out statewide. Before Pinellas County's cases were confirmed, Florida health officials had already recorded at least three locally acquired dengue cases this summer in Hillsborough, Palm Beach, and Miami-Dade counties, according to WUSF. South Florida county health departments issued their own mosquito-borne illness alerts in early August, a trend Hoodline covered in its report on dengue alerts rattling Palm Beach and Miami-Dade. Why Rain Triggers a Mosquito Boom The biology behind the sudden spike traces back to the mosquitoes themselves. Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the primary vector for dengue, lay eggs that can remain dormant in dry soil or containers for up to eight months until rain triggers hatching, WUSF reported, citing expert research on the species. That means a single heavy rain event can awaken a season's worth of dormant eggs almost simultaneously, feeding the kind of population explosion seen in Hillsborough's trap counts. Infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit dengue through their bites, and unlike many native mosquito species that feed mostly at dusk or overnight, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes bite during daylight hours. That daytime activity means routine outdoor chores and errands carry real exposure risk, not just evening hours in the yard. Florida's Recurring Dengue Problem Pinellas County's cases land within a state that has repeatedly led the continental United States in dengue activity. Florida recorded 91 locally acquired cases across 10 counties in 2024, along with more than 1,000 travel-associated infections, with Miami-Dade County leading the state that year at 50 local cases, according to Outbreak News Today. In 2025, the state recorded 62 locally acquired cases, but the geography shifted: Brevard County accounted for more than half of them with 35 cases, while Miami-Dade recorded 25, marking the first time a Central Florida county led the state in local transmission. Pinellas County Mosquito Control monitors disease risk across all 24 local municipalities using 58 designated mosquito trap sites and eight sentinel chicken coops, which are tested weekly by state health labs, according to Pinellas County Government. The sentinel chickens serve as an early warning system, flagging when viruses begin circulating in wild bird populations before they spread more widely. That surveillance network sits alongside newer technology already deployed next door — in 2025, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management partnered with the University of South Florida to deploy AI-enabled smart traps and drone mapping aimed at identifying breeding hot spots like discarded tires, a program Hoodline detailed last year. What Dengue Looks Like and How to Avoid It Dengue is a viral illness, and symptoms typically develop within 15 days of an infected mosquito bite. Health authorities note the illness generally does not cause respiratory symptoms, but it can bring high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and sometimes a rash. Dengue does not spread directly from person to person — it requires an infected mosquito to bite and transmit the virus. Health authorities are urging residents to eliminate standing water around their homes, including in buckets, flowerpots, pool covers, and trash cans, since these are common breeding sites for Aedes aegypti. Officials also recommend fixing broken screens on doors and windows, wearing loose long-sleeved clothing outdoors, and applying EPA-registered insect repellents to skin and clothing. Residents who suspect dengue symptoms are advised to contact a healthcare provider. DOH-Pinellas maintains ongoing surveillance for vector-borne pathogens across Florida, which also includes tracking for West Nile virus, chikungunya, malaria, St. Louis encephalitis, and Eastern equine encephalitis. It remains unclear which specific neighborhoods within Pinellas County the two dengue cases originated from, whether the two patients are connected in any way, or which serotype of the dengue virus was identified — questions that remain open as investigators continue their work. analysis.time: Published on August 11, 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated, but the confirmation of cases occurred this week, with prior warnings issued on August 7, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Pinellas County, Florida, with a focus on Tampa Bay. The affected population includes residents exposed to mosquito-borne dengue virus.
analysis.event: Pinellas County health officials confirmed two locally acquired cases of dengue fever. The cases are part of a broader mosquito-borne illness surge in Tampa Bay, linked to heavy summer rainstorms and increased mosquito populations. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Two confirmed dengue cases in Pinellas County. The mosquito population surge in Hillsborough County saw trap collections jump from 142 to 18,000 mosquitoes in mid-July. Dengue transmission is a concern due to the daytime biting behavior of Aedes mosquitoes, increasing exposure risk during routine outdoor activities. news.content_zh: 佛罗里达州皮内拉斯县确认了两例本地感染的 登革热 病例,这是坦帕湾地区更广泛的蚊媒疾病激增的一部分。暴发 与夏季暴雨有关,导致蚊子数量急剧增加,特别是埃及伊蚊和白纹伊蚊,它们通过叮咬传播登革热。这些蚊子在白天很活跃,增加了晚上之后的暴露风险。佛罗里达州卫生部和皮尼拉斯县蚊虫控制中心正在协调 监测 和预防工作。皮尼拉斯县蚊虫控制中心于 2026 年 8 月 7 日发布了先前的警告,强调了在病例确诊之前威胁的加剧。邻近地区希尔斯伯勒县继 7 月底出现首例登革热病例后,已于 2026 年 8 月 5 日报告了夏季第二例登革热病例。蚊子活动激增促使多轮杀虫剂治疗和有针对性的地面检查。然而,受影响的社区、患者关系和登革热血清型等具体细节仍在调查中。登革热不会直接在人与人之间传播,但需要受感染的蚊子来传播病毒。这种情况反映了佛罗里达州反复出现的问题,该州近年来在登革热活动方面领先美国,2024 年有 91 例本地感染病例,2025 年有 62 例。

news.content: Case of dengue fever confirmed in Palm Beach County. How to stay safe Someone has recently contracted dengue fever in Palm Beach County. The Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County sent an advisory about a confirmed case of the mosquito-borne illness on Aug. 3. Miami-Dade County reported a local case on the same day. “DOH-Palm Beach and Palm Beach County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts,” reads the Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County release. Dengue fever is a disease related to the viruses that cause West Nile virus and yellow fever. Several cases are reported in Florida each year from people traveling to areas that have the disease, which usually include the Caribbean, Central and South America and Asia, according to the Florida Department of Health. Cyclospora in Palm Beach County: Cyclospora cases rise in Palm Beach County. What to know on outbreak It is common in many countries around the world and almost half of the world’s population live in areas at risk of dengue, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. Still, no countries are in the CDC’s “high transmission” category for dengue fever right now. No countries have had 10 or more cases reported among travelers in the last three months as of July 1. How is dengue fever transmitted? Dengue infection is acquired through the bite of a certain species of mosquito. These include Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Both types of mosquito live in Florida. What are the symptoms of dengue fever? Dengue fever can be painful and debilitating, but it is rarely fatal, according to the Florida Department of Health. Symptoms start between three and 14 days after an infected mosquito bite. They include a sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain and bleeding. Vomiting and diarrhea are also possible. Symptoms usually last four to seven days. A more severe form of dengue is dengue hemorrhagic fever. It is rare, but it can be fatal if not treated. There is no treatment for dengue fever, but symptoms and complications can be managed. How to avoid dengue fever? People can protect themselves from getting bitten by mosquitoes. They can apply insect repellent to exposed skin or clothing, treat clothing with products containing 0.5% permethrin, be careful not to leave out standing water (where mosquitoes breed) and keep screens on windows. news.source_body_en: Florida health officials confirmed a single locally acquired dengue fever case in Palm Beach County on August 3, 2026, marking the first such report in the county this year. The Florida Department of Health and Palm Beach County Mosquito Control launched joint surveillance and vector-control measures, including targeted insecticide application and public advisories on eliminating mosquito breeding sites. While dengue is rarely fatal, symptoms can be severe, ranging from high fever and joint pain to rare but life-threatening hemorrhagic complications. Health authorities emphasized prevention through repellent use, permethrin-treated clothing, and window screens, noting that no countries are currently classified by the CDC as experiencing high dengue transmission. The case follows a simultaneous report in neighboring Miami-Dade County, underscoring ongoing regional vigilance.
news.content_zh: 佛罗里达州卫生官员于 2026 年 8 月 3 日确认棕榈滩县出现一例本地感染的 登革热 病例,这是该县今年首次报告此类病例。佛罗里达州卫生部和棕榈滩县蚊虫控制中心联合启动了 监测 和 媒介 控制措施,包括有针对性地使用杀虫剂以及消除蚊子滋生地的公共咨询。虽然登革热很少致命,但症状可能很严重,从高烧和关节疼痛到罕见但危及生命的出血并发症。卫生当局强调通过使用驱虫剂、经过氯菊酯处理的衣服和纱窗进行预防,并指出目前没有国家被疾病预防控制中心列为登革热高发国家。此案发生之前,邻近的迈阿密戴德县也同时发布了一份报告,突显了该地区持续保持警惕。

India World Sport Data Health Opinion Science Entertainment Premium Videos Podcast Photos Visual Stories Specials TH Explains eBooks TH Games Newsletter Lit For Life The Huddle Home Sci-Tech Health India’s dengue burden grows more complex as multiple virus strains circulate together, study finds The two-year nationwide surveillance study by the ICMR-VRDL network reveals increased risk of severe disease, and fresh challenges for the rollout of future dengue vaccination programmes Updated - August 07, 2026 10:54 pm IST - NEW DELHI Bindu Shajan Perappadan READ LATER SEE ALL Remove There are four dengue serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) and severity depends more on secondary infection than serotype, although DENV-2 has often been linked to severe outbreaks. File image for representation only | Photo Credit: Sandeep Saxena India may be entering a more perilous phase in its dengue epidemic, with multiple strains of the virus now circulating simultaneously across much of the country, raising concerns over an increased risk of severe disease, and posing fresh challenges for the rollout of future dengue vaccination programmes. A two-year nationwide surveillance study by the Indian Council of Medical Research’s (ICMR) Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (VRDL) network found that all four dengue virus serotypes are circulating together in several parts of the country, with nearly one in 14 patients infected with more than one serotype at the same time. India’s first dengue vaccine arrives with a crucial safety caveat The study, titled ‘Pan-India Molecular Surveillance of Dengue Serotypes, 2023–2025’, analysed 6,889 laboratory-confirmed dengue samples from 45 laboratories across 25 States and Union Territories and found that DENV-2 remained the predominant serotype, accounting for over half of all infections. However, researchers said the broader concern was the widespread co-circulation of multiple serotypes, indicating dengue hyper-endemicity. Eight States and Union Territories reported the presence of all four serotypes, while 15 reported three circulating simultaneously. Around 7% of patients were infected with two or more dengue serotypes concurrently. QDENGA: Can the new Japanese vaccine end the dengue menace in India? | In Focus Podcast The study also found that patients with concurrent infections were more likely to develop severe manifestations of dengue, including dangerously low platelet counts, bleeding complications and severe joint pain, compared with those infected with a single serotype. While the findings need confirmation through long-term clinical studies, they suggest that simultaneous infection with multiple strains could worsen disease severity. There are four dengue serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) and severity depends more on secondary infection than serotype, although DENV-2 has often been linked to severe outbreaks. The emergence of hyperendemic transmission has implications beyond clinical care, the report notes. India currently has no dengue vaccine in its Universal Immunisation Programme, although indigenous vaccine candidates are in advanced stages of clinical development, and an internationally approved vaccine recently received regulatory clearance for import and sale in India. Researchers look at biomarkers which can predict dengue severity Continuous surveillance of circulating serotypes would be critical because vaccine effectiveness varies against different dengue strains, and shifts in the dominant serotype could influence both outbreak intensity and vaccine performance, researchers said. “Apart from routine steps taken to prevent mosquito breeding, there is certainly a need to incorporate the dengue vaccine into public health programmes, initially targeting endemic areas,” Gautam Menon, Professor of Physics and Biology, Ashoka University, said, speaking about the need for continuous surveillance. “But we also need more regular studies that can alert us about the magnitude of the problem, identify hotspots, and provide early warnings on how serotypes are shifting. This should be an ongoing, regularly reported study,” he added. news.content_zh: 印度ICMR-VRDL网络开展的一项为期两年的全国性研究记录了监测(登革热)四种血清型(DENV-1至DENV-4)在多个邦同时流行的情况,其中DENV-2占主导地位。近1/14的患者同时感染一种以上血清型,这种模式与重症登革热风险增加(包括出血并发症和危险的血小板计数过低)相关。研究人员警告称,这种高度地方性流行模式使登革热防控复杂化,并为未来的疫苗接种计划带来挑战,因疫苗效果随血清型而异,且优势株变化可改变疫苗接种动态。该研究呼吁在地方性流行地区持续开展血清型监测,并采取针对性疫苗接种策略。

Advertisement Lee County on alert as dengue season ramps up in Florida Mosquito season is underway, and with it comes the heightened risk of mosquito-borne diseases like dengue. Show more Show less 2:42 2:42 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save LEE COUNTY, Fla. (WINK)—Public health officials are testing mosquitoes in Lee County as the state continues to report new cases of dengue virus. Most people who get the virus don't develop symptoms, according to the World Health Organization. However, severe cases can be deadly. The Florida Department of Health reported 55 dengue cases across the state as of Aug. 1. The vast majority of those cases came from travel, the health department said. However, four cases were recorded locally. That means they came from mosquitoes in Florida, which health researchers said is rare. Hillsborough County reported two locally transmitted cases last week. Florida has dengue cases almost every year, said Professor Michael Teng, an infectious disease researcher at the University of South Florida. It's usually imported by people who travel overseas. "There are a lot of dengue virus endemic regions in the Caribbean and South America, so it's not uncommon to see in Florida," Teng said. "I think when we start seeing local transmission of the virus, then we start to worry a little bit because that's the way we can get an outbreak of the virus." Researchers are keeping an eye on the localized cases, Teng said, but they aren't a concern just yet. The only major Florida outbreak was between 2009 and 2010 on Key West, when 28 cases were reported. That doesn't stop local officials from keeping an eye out. "We literally are always on alert," said Jenifer McBride, communications director for the Lee County Mosquito Control District. When there is a confirmed or suspected case of dengue, the district will use specialized trucks to spray the neighborhood, McBride said. Lee County reported two cases of dengue so far this year, according to the Florida Department of Health. Both came from international travel. The district also said it proactively tests mosquitoes in a lab at its Buckingham headquarters. Mosquitoes are trapped and brought back to the lab for immediate results. The lab will grind up mosquitoes and run them through a test to see if they're carrying specific diseases. The district will often test Aedes aegypti mosquitoes - known as the backyard mosquito. That species can transmit other diseases, Teng said, including the chikungunya and Zika virus. "We rely on our community members really to make sure that they're dumping out the standing water in their backyard," McBride said. "That helps us tremendously." analysis.brief_en: Florida health authorities are on heightened alert as the state reports 55 dengue cases through August 2026, including four locally transmitted infections—two in Hillsborough County and none in Lee County. While most cases are travel-related, the presence of local transmission signals a rare but growing risk as mosquito season peaks. Lee County, which has recorded two travel-associated cases this year, has stepped up surveillance by testing trapped mosquitoes in a dedicated lab and stands ready to conduct neighborhood spraying if needed. Public health experts note that severe dengue can be fatal and that Aedes aegypti—the ‘backyard mosquito’—can also carry chikungunya and Zika, underscoring the importance of eliminating standing water. Researchers stress that localized cases are being watched closely but do not yet constitute an outbreak.

news.content: ULTIMATE VOTER GUIDE to candidates, issues, debates News Sports Opinion Email Us Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Dengue one of 8 Florida mosquito-borne diseases. Symptoms to watch for Mosquito-borne illness advisories and alerts have been issued for some Florida counties Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Aug. 7, 2026, 10:55 a.m. ET Florida's Department of Health monitors mosquito-borne illnesses in the state. Symptoms of eight mosquito-borne illnesses seen in Florida. Mosquito-borne illness advisories and alerts have been issued for some Florida counties. Is there anything more annoying than mosquitoes when you're trying to enjoy the outdoors in Florida? Hm, now that we think about it, yes: Mosquitoes slipping into your home and buzzing you as you're trying to sleep! That's bad enough, but mosquitoes bring with them diseases, making them the world's deadliest animal. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents Florida's Department of Health monitors mosquito-borne illnesses in the state, and there are several of them. Four cases of dengue were reported in the state in July. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for and how best to prevent mosquito bites. How many types of mosquito-borne illnesses are there in Florida? FDOH compiles weekly data on the following mosquito-borne viruses in a report called "Florida Arbovirus Surveillance": West Nile virus (WNV) Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV) St. Louis encephalitis virus (SLEV) Dengue virus (DENV) Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) Zika virus (ZIKV) California encephalitis group viruses (CEV) Malaria Mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Leon Palm Beach Pasco A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Hillsborough Miami-Dade "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." How many cases of mosquito-borne illnesses have been reported in Florida this year? According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Aug. 1, the following number of cases of mosquito-borne illnesses acquired in Florida have been reported: West Nile 1 in Alachua County 1 asymptomatic blood donor in Leon County Dengue 2 in Hillsborough County 1 in Miami-Dade County 1 in Palm Beach County What are symptoms of dengue fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually lasts four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses." What are symptoms of West Nile virus? "West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that causes mild to severe illness," the Florida Department of Health said. "Approximately 80% of people who are infected with WNV will not show any symptoms at all." Mild symptoms include: fever headache body aches nausea vomiting Sometimes swollen lymph glands or a skin rash on the chest, stomach and back. Symptoms can last from a few days to several weeks. About one in 150 people infected with West Nile will develop severe illness. Symptoms include: high fever headache neck stiffness stupor disorientation coma tremors convulsions muscle weakness vision loss numbness paralysis "These symptoms may last several weeks, and neurological effects may be permanent. Severe illness can also result in death," FDOH said. What are symptoms of Eastern equine encephalitis virus? Most people infected with eastern equine encephalitis virus do not develop symptoms, according to the Florida Department of Health. For those who develop symptoms, the time from an infected mosquito bite to onset of illness ranges from four to 10 days. The CDC said symptoms of a mild illness include: fever chills body aches joint pain neurologic disease Symptoms of severe illness can include meningitis or encephalitis: fever headache vomiting diarrhea seizures behavioral changes drowsiness coma What are symptoms of St. Louis encephalitis virus? Most people infected with St. Louis encephalitis virus do not have symptoms, according to the Florida Department of Health. Symptoms of those who do become ill include: fever headache nausea vomiting tiredness What are symptoms of Chikungunya virus? Up to 28% of people who are infected with the Chikungunya virus will not have any symptoms, according to the Florida Department of Health. Symptoms of those who do can include: sudden high fever (usually higher than 102o F) which may be continuous or intermittent Severe joint pain that commonly involves the hands and feet Joint swelling Back pain Rash usually 2-5 days after fever starts Other symptoms may include headache, body ache, nausea, vomiting, and redness around the eyes. In unusual cases, infection can involve the brain, eyes, heart, kidney, and other organs "Fatal infections are rare, however many patients have chronic joint pain, arthritis, loss of energy, and depression lasting weeks to years," FDOH said. What are symptoms of Zika virus ? Many people infected with Zika virus will not have symptoms or will only have mild symptoms, according to the Florida Department of Health. Common symptoms of Zika include: fever rash headache joint pain conjunctivitis (red eyes) "Zika symptoms usually last for several days to a week," FDOH said. "People usually do not get sick enough to go to the hospital. For this reason, many people might not realize they have been infected." What are symptoms of California encephalitis group viruses? Most people infected with California serogroup viruses have no symptoms, according to the Mayo Clinic. Symptoms include: fever sore throat headache gastrointestinal symptoms What are symptoms of malaria? Symptoms of malaria depend on the type of parasite carried by the infected mosquito. In most cases, symptoms develop between seven and 30 days after the bite. Some symptoms may not appear up to a year later and, if not treated properly, can cause additional attacks, according to the Florida Department of Health. Common symptoms include such flu-like symptoms such as: fever chills sweats headache nausea vomiting body aches general malaise A bite by a mosquito carrying the Plasmodium falciparum parasite can cause severe and life-threatening disease. What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient Drain and cover helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. news.content: Virulent dengue strain circulating in Delhi: Officials Civic authorities said they have intensified anti-larvae drives and heightened vigilance for mosquito-borne diseases after a particularly virulent strain of dengue, type-2, has been found to be in circulation in the Capital Published on: Aug 12, 2026, 08:09:31 IST By Paras Singh Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link Civic authorities said they have intensified anti-larvae drives and heightened vigilance for mosquito-borne diseases after a particularly virulent strain of dengue, type-2, has been found to be in circulation in the Capital. Virulent dengue strain circulating in Delhi: Officials A senior civic official said that genome sequencing of dengue-positive samples in Delhi has shown that the dengue virus type 2 (DENV-2) strain was found in a majority of the cases.Officials did not share details, including how many samples were sequenced and how many of them were type-2. No deaths, however, have been recorded so far this year. “Dengue has multiple strains. Type 1 can cause classic dengue fever along with chills and headaches while Type 2 can lead to haemorrhagic fever with shock and chills,” the official explained. Individuals with weak immune systems, such as the elderly, children and those with chronic illnesses, are particularly vulnerable. “We are still in the initial phase of the monsoon cycle and focusing on destruction at the larval stages,” the official added. Confirming this, mayor Parwesh Wahi said, “We have issued directions to increase the fogging in vulnerable areas and hospital beds have been reserved in MCD run hospitals. Anti-larvae drives are being intensified.” Five-year municipal data on detection of mosquito breeding shows that the weekly count of mosquito larvae detection peaks between 32nd and 38th week of the year. With incessant rain, the breeding rate has increased over the last fortnight. “The mosquito causing dengue breeds in clear water and waterlogged areas and the primary method of preventing the dengue is through breeding site reduction. With regular rain spells over the last 10 days, waterlogging has increased in various parts of the city,” the official quoted above added. MCD does not maintain data on strains. They come from tests carried out by AIIMS. MCD action taken report recorded 9,803 sites with larvae over the last week, around 12% of the overall positive sites (82,870) detected between January 1 and August 8 this year. According to MCD’s weekly vector-borne disease report dated August 8, at least 230 dengue cases have been reported so far in this year with an additional 76 cases where infection was acquired from other states. In 159 cases, the address of the patient was wrong or they could not be found. However, the figures do not match health minister Pankaj Kumar Singh’s report after a review last week. “So far, a total of 1,179 dengue cases have been reported in Delhi. From the NCR region, outside Delhi, around 210–212 cases have been reported,” he said. MCD officials did not respond to HT requests for comment on the discrepancy in the data. According to MCD data from previous years, 315 cases were reported in 2025, 322 in 2024, 244 cases in 2023, and 64 cases in 2022 during the corresponding period. The civic body had officially stopped making weekly vector-borne disease reports public ahead of the G20 summit in Delhi. Type 2 was in circulation at the time. Type 2 strain was also predominant during the city’s worst dengue outbreak in 2015 when 15,867 cases and 60 deaths were reported due to dengue over 12 months. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. While it is typically not fatal and most people do not develop symptoms, those who do typically experience high fever, headache, body aches, nausea, and rash. Most recover within 1-2 weeks, but it can be fatal in extreme cases. Delhi saw four confirmed dengue-related deaths in 2025, 11 in 2024, 19 in 2023, and nine cases in 2022. ABOUT THE AUTHOR Paras Singh Paras Singh is a New Delhi-based journalist with Hindustan Times, where he serves as Deputy Metro Editor. He reports on urban governance, the Delhi government, the Delhi BJP, water management, the environment, communities and city life. He joined Hindustan Times in 2021 after beginning his journalism career at The Times of India in 2016, where he covered civic bodies, the water and power sectors, and urban infrastructure. Over the last decade, some of his reporting has led to significant public impact, with investigations into environmental violations, corruption and illegal industrial activity contributing to multiple judicial interventions by the National Green Tribunal and the Delhi High Court. A graduate of St. Stephen's College, University of Delhi, Paras studied journalism from the Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC), New Delhi. Having extensively covered the capital's evolving civic and governance landscape, his recent work increasingly explores Delhi's history, built heritage, urban evolution and the relationship between people and place, alongside continuing to report on governance and public policy. news.title_zh: 官员:德里流行致命登革热菌株德里最新消息 - 印度斯坦时报
news.source_body_en: A virulent dengue strain, specifically type-2, has been identified as circulating in Delhi, according to officials. This was confirmed through genome sequencing of dengue-positive samples, though details on the number of samples tested were not provided. The report notes that no deaths have been recorded so far this year, but the type-2 strain is known to cause more severe symptoms, including haemorrhagic fever with shock. Officials have intensified anti-larvae drives and increased fogging in vulnerable areas to combat the spread of the virus. The MCD has reserved hospital beds in its-run hospitals and is focusing on larval destruction during the monsoon cycle. However, there is a discrepancy in the reported case numbers between the MCD and the health minister’s data, with the MCD reporting 230 cases in Delhi and 76 from other states. The report also highlights that individuals with weak immune systems, such as the elderly and children, are particularly vulnerable to the virus. The MCD has stopped publishing weekly vector-borne disease reports ahead of the G20 summit, adding to the uncertainty in the current situation.

news.content_title: Two Locally Acquired Dengue Cases Confirmed In Pinellas County
news.content: PINELLAS COUNTY, Fla. – Health officials in Pinellas County have confirmed two local cases of dengue fever, prompting response efforts to control the area’s mosquito population. The Florida Department of Health in Pinellas County announced it is coordinating surveillance and prevention measures alongside Pinellas County Mosquito Control. Vector control strategies currently underway include increased truck fogging, aerial larviciding, and targeted ground inspections to locate and eliminate potential breeding grounds. Dengue is a viral illness transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. It does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms typically develop within 15 days of a bite and include high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and occasionally a rash. Unlike many seasonal viruses, dengue generally does not cause respiratory symptoms. To reduce the risk of transmission, health authorities advise residents to eliminate standing water around homes by emptying items like buckets, flowerpots, pool covers, and trash cans. Additional recommendations include fixing broken screens on doors and windows, wearing loose long-sleeved clothing, and applying EPA-registered insect repellents to skin and clothing. DOH-Pinellas notes that state health agencies maintain ongoing surveillance for multiple vector-borne pathogens across Florida, including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria, chikungunya, and dengue. Residents who suspect they are experiencing symptoms of dengue are advised to contact a healthcare provider. news.content_title: Mosquito Alert: Eighth Local Dengue Case Confirmed In Hillsborough County
news.content: HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. – Health officials in Hillsborough County have confirmed an eighth human case of locally acquired dengue fever, keeping the region under an ongoing mosquito-borne illness alert. The Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County (DOH-Hillsborough) announced the diagnosis and stated that it is coordinating with Hillsborough County Mosquito Management to deploy surveillance and prevention resources to curb local mosquito populations. Dengue fever is a viral infection transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. It is not contagious between humans. Symptoms typically develop within 15 days of an infected bite and can include a sudden fever, severe muscle and joint aches, and a rash. Unlike typical flu viruses, dengue generally does not cause respiratory symptoms. To reduce the risk of transmission, health officials advise residents to take preventative steps against mosquito bites and breeding: Drain standing water: Empty water from items such as tires, buckets, flowerpots, pool covers, and coolers. According to DOH-Hillsborough, a single water-filled tire can serve as a breeding ground for hundreds of mosquitoes. Cover exposed skin: Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants when outdoors. Use insect repellent: Apply EPA-registered repellents to skin and clothing as directed. EPA-registered repellents are tested and approved as safe for general use, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Secure homes: Repair damaged window, door, porch, and patio screens to prevent mosquitoes from entering indoor spaces. DOH-Hillsborough continues statewide monitoring for various mosquito-borne pathogens, including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria, chikungunya, and dengue. Residents are also encouraged to report dead bird sightings through the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission website to assist with broader disease surveillance across the state. Video above: See the week's top headlines in Tampa Bay PINELLAS COUNTY, Fla. (WFLA) — Pinellas County is ramping up its mosquito removal efforts after the Florida Department of Health reported two locally acquired cases of dengue fever. The county health department announced the confirmed cases on Tuesday afternoon and said it is coordinating treatment plans with Pinellas County Mosquito Control. Residents may notice an increase in truck fogging, aerial spraying, and ground inspections of potential breeding locations as the county works to reduce mosquito populations. Advertisement Advertisement 20+ Border Collies removed from feces-covered home of former Florida breeder: sheriff The county said efforts will be concentrated in the Palm Harbor area, but residents across Pinellas are advised to take precautions. Truck fogging data from the county shows much of Palm Harbor was treated Tuesday morning. Parts of St. Petersburg, Clearwater, Safety Harbor and Oldsmar were also treated over the last few days, particularly areas along Tampa Bay. You can visit this site to see recent treatments in your area. Symptoms of dengue fever can include flu-like symptoms such as muscle aches, joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash, DOH said. Advertisement Advertisement Mother of 2 kidnapped, killed by Pinellas County deputy who took his own life, sheriff says The disease is not contagious and is transmitted by bites from Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which are active during the day and breed in containers, the DOH said. Residents can help protect themselves by dumping out any standing water that may collect on their property. Additionally, dressing in light-colored, long-sleeved clothing and using insect repellent can help prevent bites. news.content: 🌍 Your Global Travel News Source Travel & Transportation AboutContactPrivacy Policy ☰ NEWS Travel NewsAirline NewsAirlines ✈️Hotel NewsCruise NewsDestinationsTravel DealsTravel Alerts Home✈️ Airline HubsTravel NewsTourism NewsAirline NewsTravel Association NewsRailway NewsCruise NewsDestination NewsHotel NewsMeeting and Event IndustryTravel AlertTravel DealsTravel Trends and FocusTechnology NewsTravel Events NewsAboutContact Discover more Travel Alert Zoos, Aquariums & Preserves travel alert Home›travel alert›US Issues Kenya Travel Health Alert Following Rise in Dengue Cases travel alert US Issues Kenya Travel Health Alert Following Rise in Dengue Cases The US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) issues a travel health notice for Kenya due to rising dengue cases in coastal areas and safari parks. Geographic Reference By Kunal K Choudhary August 06, 2026 4 min read Image generated by AI The US Centers for Disease Control has issued a travel health notice for Kenya due to rising cases of dengue fever, particularly in popular coastal destinations and national parks. Health Centers for Disease Control Issues Kenya Dengue Warning Health authorities have advised international visitors to take strict precautions against mosquito bites when traveling through East Africa's leading tourism hubs. According to travel advisories from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), dengue has emerged as a key travel-related risk in Kenya. The alert encourages travelers to maintain continuous mosquito protection, particularly because the Aedes mosquitoes that transmit the virus are active primarily during daylight hours. The health notice does not advise against visiting the country, but instead emphasizes prevention, early symptom recognition, and medical preparation. Outbreaks are linked to warmer temperatures, rising mosquito populations, and increased international passenger traffic. For travelers planning safaris or beach holidays, understanding the transmission environment is essential to preventing infection. High-Risk Areas and Environmental Transmission Vectors In Kenya, dengue activity has historically concentrated in regions where climate conditions support mosquito breeding. Coastal areas, including Mombasa and other destinations along the Indian Ocean, face higher risk profiles due to their warm, humid tropical environments. Health Conditions Urban centers also present challenges as Aedes mosquitoes breed in containers holding standing water near hotels, residential areas, and public parks. Travelers on outdoor walking tours, beach excursions, and safari drives are exposed to higher daytime bite risks. The Kenya Ministry of Health continues to monitor regional disease vectors to protect both local communities and international arrivals. Essential Health Advisory and Travel Insurance Safeguards For the affected traveler, the issuance of a travel health notice has direct implications for health preparation and trip protection: Travel Insurance Coverage: Standard travel insurance policies generally do not permit travelers to cancel a trip due to "fear of travel" related to a health advisory. To recover non-refundable booking costs for cancellations based on health alerts, travelers must purchase Cancel for Any Reason (CFAR) coverage, which is usually only available shortly after making initial trip deposits. Emergency Medical Care: If a traveler contracts dengue while in Kenya, standard travel medical insurance will cover diagnostic tests, emergency consultations, and hospitalization costs, provided the policy lacks exclusions for tropical infections. Symptom Awareness: Common symptoms include high fever, severe headaches, pain behind the eyes, joint and muscle pain, skin rash, and nausea. Returning travelers who develop these symptoms should seek immediate medical attention and disclose their travel history. Medication Warning: Travelers showing symptoms of dengue should avoid taking aspirin or ibuprofen, as these medications can increase bleeding risks associated with severe dengue. Paracetamol should be used instead. Impact on East Africa's Tourism Growth and Health Security The travel health notice arrives as Kenya continues to expand its position in the global safari and beach tourism sectors. Wildlife conservation reserves and luxury eco-lodges attract millions of visitors annually, making safety communication essential to maintaining visitor confidence. Zoos, Aquariums & Preserves Addressing mosquito-borne disease risks requires ongoing coordination between tourism operators, municipal health boards, and international agencies. Hotels and lodges in high-risk zones have implemented preventative spraying and screened accommodations to protect guests. Travelers who prepare appropriate insect repellent containing DEET or picaridin, pack protective long-sleeved clothing, and choose screened lodging can continue to safely explore the country's diverse wildlife parks. Coastal areas, including Mombasa and other destinations along the Indian Ocean, face higher risk profiles due to their warm, humid tropical environments. Health Conditions Urban centers also present challenges as Aedes mosquitoes breed in containers holding standing water near hotels, residential areas, and public parks. Travelers on outdoor walking tours, beach excursions, and safari drives are exposed to higher daytime bite risks. The Kenya Ministry of Health continues to monitor regional disease vectors to protect both local communities and international arrivals. Essential Health Advisory and Travel Insurance Safeguards For the affected traveler, the issuance of a travel health notice has direct implications for health preparation and trip protection: Travel Insurance Coverage: Standard travel insurance policies generally do not permit travelers to cancel a trip due to "fear of travel" related to a health advisory. To recover non-refundable booking costs for cancellations based on health alerts, travelers must purchase Cancel for Any Reason (CFAR) coverage, which is usually only available shortly after making initial trip deposits. Emergency Medical Care: If a traveler contracts dengue while in Kenya, standard travel medical insurance will cover diagnostic tests, emergency consultations, and hospitalization costs, provided the policy lacks exclusions for tropical infections. Symptom Awareness: Common symptoms include high fever, severe headaches, pain behind the eyes, joint and muscle pain, skin rash, and nausea. Returning travelers who develop these symptoms should seek immediate medical attention and disclose their travel history. Medication Warning: Travelers showing symptoms of dengue should avoid taking aspirin or ibuprofen, as these medications can increase bleeding risks associated with severe dengue. Paracetamol should be used instead. Impact on East Africa's Tourism Growth and Health Security The travel health notice arrives as Kenya continues to expand its position in the global safari and beach tourism sectors. Wildlife conservation reserves and luxury eco-lodges attract millions of visitors annually, making safety communication essential to maintaining visitor confidence. Zoos, Aquariums & Preserves Addressing mosquito-borne disease risks requires ongoing coordination between tourism operators, municipal health boards, and international agencies. Hotels and lodges in high-risk zones have implemented preventative spraying and screened accommodations to protect guests. Travelers who prepare appropriate insect repellent containing DEET or picaridin, pack protective long-sleeved clothing, and choose screened lodging can continue to safely explore the country's diverse wildlife parks. Health By Preeti Gunjan August 06, 2026 4 min read Image generated by AI General Reference The United States has issued a formal travel health alert for Kenya following a surge in dengue fever cases. While the country remains open for tourism, health officials are urging visitors to implement strict preventative measures to avoid mosquito-borne infections. US CDC Issues Warning Over Dengue Transmission in Kenya The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has identified dengue fever as a significant travel-related health risk for those visiting Kenya. The alert emphasizes that mosquito-borne diseases are prevalent not only in the country's famous coastal resorts but also within major urban centers and expansive game parks. Unlike many other mosquito species that are primarily active at night, the Aedes mosquitoes responsible for transmitting dengue are active during daylight hours. This means travelers are at risk throughout the day, necessitating continuous protection regardless of the time. Despite the alert, US officials have clarified that travel to Kenya should not be avoided. The guidance is intended to ensure that international visitors—who may have lower natural immunity to tropical diseases—approach their trips with informed preparation and early awareness. Health Conditions High-Risk Zones and Transmission Factors Dengue fever is increasingly becoming a global health challenge, driven by rising global temperatures, rapid urban growth, and the fluidity of international travel. In Kenya, the risk is concentrated in environments where mosquito breeding is most favorable. Coastal Regions: Areas surrounding Mombasa and other Indian Ocean destinations are high-risk due to the warm, humid climate. Urban Centers: Cities face elevated risks as mosquitoes frequently breed in stagnant water found in containers near hotels, public spaces, and residential neighborhoods. Outdoor Tourism Hubs: Visitors engaging in walking tours, beach activities, and nature reserve explorations are more exposed to bites. Recognizing Dengue Fever: Symptoms and Medical Risks Dengue is a viral infection that can vary from mild discomfort to life-threatening complications. Because the symptoms often mimic other tropical illnesses, early medical intervention and a detailed travel history are vital for an accurate diagnosis. Tourist Destinations Common Symptoms Include: High fever and severe headaches Pain located behind the eyes Acute joint and muscle pain Skin rashes Nausea, vomiting, and general fatigue While most patients recover with rest and medical care, some develop "severe dengue." This critical stage can lead to internal bleeding, respiratory distress, and dangerously low blood pressure. Essential Prevention Strategies for 2026 Travelers To mitigate the risk of infection, the CDC recommends a multi-layered approach to protection. Relying on a single method is often insufficient in high-transmission zones. Travel & Transportation Chemical and Physical Barriers Travelers should use insect repellents containing approved active ingredients such as DEET or picaridin. Additionally, wearing long-sleeved shirts, long trousers, and closed-toe footwear is recommended to minimize exposed skin. Strategic Accommodation When booking hotels or lodges, prioritize facilities that offer: Air conditioning to keep mosquitoes out of living spaces. Screened windows and doors. Active mosquito prevention and pest control systems. Environmental Awareness Avoid spending extended time near standing water, such as garden ponds or drainage areas, which serve as primary breeding grounds for the Aedes mosquito. Health Impact on Kenya's Tourism Infrastructure Kenya continues to be a premier global destination, and the health alert has not led to the closure of any major attractions. The tourism sector remains fully operational, with luxury safari lodges and coastal resorts maintaining standard safety protocols. The current situation underscores a broader shift in global travel: the integration of health security into the planning process. Travelers are now prioritizing disease alerts and vaccination schedules as much as itinerary planning. Health By Preeti Gunjan August 06, 2026 4 min read Image generated by AI General Reference The United States has issued a formal travel health alert for Kenya following a surge in dengue fever cases. While the country remains open for tourism, health officials are urging visitors to implement strict preventative measures to avoid mosquito-borne infections. US CDC Issues Warning Over Dengue Transmission in Kenya The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has identified dengue fever as a significant travel-related health risk for those visiting Kenya. The alert emphasizes that mosquito-borne diseases are prevalent not only in the country's famous coastal resorts but also within major urban centers and expansive game parks. Unlike many other mosquito species that are primarily active at night, the Aedes mosquitoes responsible for transmitting dengue are active during daylight hours. This means travelers are at risk throughout the day, necessitating continuous protection regardless of the time. Despite the alert, US officials have clarified that travel to Kenya should not be avoided. The guidance is intended to ensure that international visitors—who may have lower natural immunity to tropical diseases—approach their trips with informed preparation and early awareness. Health Conditions High-Risk Zones and Transmission Factors Dengue fever is increasingly becoming a global health challenge, driven by rising global temperatures, rapid urban growth, and the fluidity of international travel. In Kenya, the risk is concentrated in environments where mosquito breeding is most favorable. Coastal Regions: Areas surrounding Mombasa and other Indian Ocean destinations are high-risk due to the warm, humid climate. Urban Centers: Cities face elevated risks as mosquitoes frequently breed in stagnant water found in containers near hotels, public spaces, and residential neighborhoods. Outdoor Tourism Hubs: Visitors engaging in walking tours, beach activities, and nature reserve explorations are more exposed to bites. Recognizing Dengue Fever: Symptoms and Medical Risks Dengue is a viral infection that can vary from mild discomfort to life-threatening complications. Because the symptoms often mimic other tropical illnesses, early medical intervention and a detailed travel history are vital for an accurate diagnosis. Tourist Destinations Common Symptoms Include: High fever and severe headaches Pain located behind the eyes Acute joint and muscle pain Skin rashes Nausea, vomiting, and general fatigue While most patients recover with rest and medical care, some develop "severe dengue." This critical stage can lead to internal bleeding, respiratory distress, and dangerously low blood pressure. Essential Prevention Strategies for 2026 Travelers To mitigate the risk of infection, the CDC recommends a multi-layered approach to protection. Relying on a single method is often insufficient in high-transmission zones. Travel & Transportation Chemical and Physical Barriers Travelers should use insect repellents containing approved active ingredients such as DEET or picaridin. Additionally, wearing long-sleeved shirts, long trousers, and closed-toe footwear is recommended to minimize exposed skin. Strategic Accommodation When booking hotels or lodges, prioritize facilities that offer: Air conditioning to keep mosquitoes out of living spaces. Screened windows and doors. Active mosquito prevention and pest control systems. Environmental Awareness Avoid spending extended time near standing water, such as garden ponds or drainage areas, which serve as primary breeding grounds for the Aedes mosquito. Health Impact on Kenya's Tourism Infrastructure Kenya continues to be a premier global destination, and the health alert has not led to the closure of any major attractions. The tourism sector remains fully operational, with luxury safari lodges and coastal resorts maintaining standard safety protocols. The current situation underscores a broader shift in global travel: the integration of health security into the planning process. Travelers are now prioritizing disease alerts and vaccination schedules as much as itinerary planning. news.content: Wednesday, August 12, 2026 18°C•Cloudy8 km/hNairobi Notifications blocked LoginRegister Search HomePoliticsBusinessOpinionSportsExplainersCryptocurrencyCulture & SocietyFeaturesNewsTechPodcastsVideosBlockchain SomaliaKenyaDjiboutiEthiopiaEritrea SomaliaKenyaDjiboutiEthiopiaEritrea US Issues Dengue Alert for Travellers Visiting Parts of Kenya as Cases Continue to Rise August 6, 2026 3 min read By Benadeta Mwaura - Reporter Kenya, August 6, 2026 - The United States has issued a fresh health advisory warning travellers about the risk of dengue fever in parts of Kenya following a rise in infections, placing the country back on the list of destinations under the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) global dengue surveillance programme. The alert, issued through the US Embassy in Nairobi and the CDC, identifies Kenya's coastal region as well as the northeastern counties of Wajir and Garissa as areas of concern. Although the notice does not advise Americans against travelling to Kenya, it urges visitors to take precautions to protect themselves against mosquito bites. According to the CDC, Kenya remains under a Level One advisory category, meaning travellers are advised to practise normal precautions while remaining alert to the risk of infection. "Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in tropical and subtropical climates that can lead to fever, aches and pains, nausea and rashes," the agency said. The CDC further advised travellers to use insect repellents, wear long-sleeved clothing and sleep in screened or air-conditioned rooms to minimise the risk of exposure. Kenya is one of 11 countries included in the latest global advisory following an increase in reported infections and concerns over the growing number of cases among travellers returning to the United States. The other countries listed are Bolivia, Cambodia, Colombia, Malaysia, the Maldives, New Caledonia, Samoa, Sri Lanka, Tonga and Vietnam. Health experts say dengue fever is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which thrive in warm, humid environments and commonly breed in stagnant water. Symptoms typically appear between three and ten days after infection and may include high fever, severe headaches, muscle and joint pain, skin rashes, nausea and, in some cases, bleeding from the nose or gums. Severe infections can lead to life-threatening complications if not treated promptly. Kenya's current outbreak is believed to have started in late 2025, although the country has experienced several previous outbreaks over the past four decades, particularly in coastal regions. Major outbreaks were reported in the early 1980s, between 2013 and 2014 and again in 2021. Public health officials have long warned that rising temperatures, rapid urbanisation and changing rainfall patterns are creating favourable conditions for the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. Unlike some countries, Kenya has not yet incorporated widespread dengue vaccination into its national immunisation programmes, making prevention and early diagnosis the country's primary line of defence. The latest advisory comes at a time when Kenya is recording increased international arrivals, with tourism authorities continuing efforts to attract more visitors to the country's beaches, wildlife parks and cultural heritage sites. Officials are therefore expected to intensify surveillance and public awareness campaigns in the affected regions. Bangladesh Dengue Outbreak Worsens, Death Toll Rises To 59 As Cases Near 18,000 Date 2026-08-08 02:00:31 Share on Facebook Tweet on Twitter (MENAFN- IANS) Dhaka, Aug 8 (IANS) As Bangladesh grapples with a worsening dengue outbreak, at least 59 people have died from the disease, while 17,880 cases have been reported so far this year, local media reported citing data from the country's Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). According to DGHS data, Dhaka division has emerged as Bangladesh's worst affected region, recording 6,871 cases this year, including 4,404 infections in Dhaka city alone. City & Local Guides With 3,647 cases, Barishal division accounted for the second-highest number of infections, followed by Chattogram with 3,082 and Khulna with 2,272. Additionally, Dhaka division topped the list for dengue fatalities, with 26 deaths, 25 of which were reported in Dhaka city. Khulna recorded the second-highest death toll at 12, followed by Chattogram and Mymensingh with seven and six deaths, respectively, Bangladesh's leading newspaper The Daily Star reported. Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, has emerged as a serious public health concern in Bangladesh. It is primarily transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. GM Saifur Rahman, Associate Professor in the Department of Zoology at the National University of Bangladesh, said that the latest figure reflects Dhaka's combination of high population density, persistent Aedes mosquito breeding, and inadequate vector control measures. The combination of high population density, warm climate and abundant breeding grounds reportedly provides ideal conditions for both Aedes mosquitoes and the dengue virus to circulate year-round, turning the Dhaka division into a major dengue hotspot. Infectious Diseases “Just a few days ago, while supervising an examination at Central Metropolitan Women's College, I found Aedes mosquito larvae in a small container of water. Such breeding sites are common across the city, indicating that Aedes mosquitoes are reproducing continuously in residential areas,” The Daily Star quoted Saifur as saying. Stressing that the mosquito control measures have been largely reactive rather than preventive, he further said,“The most effective strategy would be to intensify mosquito control during periods when dengue transmission is relatively low. At that time, breeding sites are fewer, and interventions can be more effective. Instead, mosquito control usually intensifies only after the dengue season begins, by which time infections are already increasing rapidly.” According to Saifur, Bangladesh's failure to establish an effective, centralised mosquito control mechanism has worsened the country's dengue situation. He called for the formation of a national mosquito control authority staffed with expert entomologists to coordinate, monitor and oversee vector control measures nationwide. “Until we establish a coordinated national control system, dengue cases are likely to continue rising,” he warned. Infectious Diseases Kabirul Bashar, Professor of the Zoology Department at Jahangirnagar University, warned that dengue infections are expected to surge through August and could continue their upward trajectory into September. “The peak may not occur in August. It's possible that this year's peak will come in September. What we can say is that the upward trend is likely to continue through August and into September,” he said. news.content: by PERPETUA ETYANG Friday August 7, 2026 Image generated with AI The United States has issued a travel health alert for Kenya following a rise in dengue fever cases, urging travellers to take extra precautions against mosquito bites. In a health alert issued by the US Embassy in Nairobi, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) listed Kenya among countries reporting a higher number of dengue cases in its updated Travel Health Notice. The advisory identifies Kenya's coastal region, as well as Wajir and Garissa counties, as areas where travellers should exercise caution. "Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in tropical and subtropical climates that can lead to fever, aches and pains, nausea, and rashes," the embassy said. The embassy urged travellers to consult the CDC's travel health advisories before travelling to affected areas and to take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Recommended precautions include using an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long trousers when outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms or rooms fitted with window screens. The alert comes as health authorities continue to monitor dengue infections in several parts of the country, with the disease primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The US Embassy advised travellers seeking more information to consult the CDC's travel health guidance or contact the agency directly before visiting affected areas. Dengue is a viral infection that affects millions of people worldwide and is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Once diagnosed, it is important to follow medical advice closely, monitor symptoms, and prioritise rest. Adequate hydration plays a crucial role in preventing complications, while nutritious meals help support the body's recovery process. Patients should remain alert to warning signs that may indicate worsening illness and seek immediate medical assistance when necessary. In some cases, hospitalisation may be recommended to ensure close monitoring and appropriate treatment during the recovery period. In May, Garissa county embarked on a massive fumigation exercise aimed at containing the spread of dengue fever following a recent outbreak that has seen several residents hospitalised at the Garissa County Referral Hospital. The two-week exercise, which officially kicked off on Thursday, will involve public health officials fumigating drainage areas, public institutions, schools, markets and other public spaces across Garissa township in an effort to eliminate mosquitoes responsible for spreading the disease. Health officials said samples taken from patients admitted at the Garissa County Referral Hospital confirmed infections of dengue fever, a viral disease transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which commonly breeds in stagnant water. Speaking to the press after overseeing the launch of the fumigation exercise, Hassan Abdullahi, who was representing the Medical Officer of Health said laboratory tests conducted at the National Public Health Laboratory confirmed the outbreak after 28 out of 40 samples collected from both public and private health facilities tested positive for dengue fever

The alert specifically highlights Kenya's coastal region, Wajir, and Garissa counties as areas of concern. Health authorities in Garissa confirmed dengue infections through laboratory tests at the Garissa County Referral Hospital and the National Public Health Laboratory, with 28 out of 40 samples testing positive. The outbreak has led to hospitalisations, prompting a two-week fumigation exercise to eliminate Aedes mosquitoes. The US Embassy recommends consulting the CDC's travel health advisories and using EPA-registered insect repellent, wearing protective clothing, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms. Patients are advised to monitor symptoms, prioritise rest, and seek immediate medical assistance if warning signs appear. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, which breed in stagnant water, and can cause fever, aches, and nausea, with potential for severe complications.

Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Tampa/ Crime & Emergencies Pinellas County Confirms Two Dengue Cases as Tampa Bay Mosquito Surge Widens By James Rodriguez Published on August 11, 2026 Source: Unsplash/ National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Pinellas County health officials confirmed two locally acquired cases of dengue fever this week, adding the county to a growing list of Tampa Bay communities grappling with mosquito-borne illness after a summer of heavy rain. The cases mark a new front in a season that has already stretched vector control teams across the region, with fogging trucks, aerial larviciding, and ground inspections underway to knock down mosquito populations before more people get sick. The confirmation, first reported by the Tampa Free Press, comes just days after neighboring Hillsborough County confirmed its own second locally acquired dengue case of the summer on August 5, following an initial case in late July, according to the Tampa Bay Times. That report noted the surge is tied to a dramatic jump in mosquito populations, with trap collections in Hillsborough County rocketing from 142 mosquitoes in a single trap in June to roughly 18,000 mosquitoes in mid-July following summer rainstorms. Hillsborough officials responded with multiple rounds of aerial and truck insecticide treatments, the newspaper reported. The Florida Department of Health in Pinellas County said it is coordinating dengue surveillance and prevention measures with Pinellas County Mosquito Control, which participates in the broader effort to track and contain the virus locally. In response to the new cases, vector control teams increased truck fogging, conducted aerial larviciding, and carried out targeted ground inspections to find and eliminate potential mosquito breeding sites. Warning Signs Came Before the Diagnoses Pinellas County Mosquito Control had already flagged rising risk days earlier. On August 7, the agency issued a public advisory warning that mosquito-borne virus transmission had increased locally following heavy summer rains, per Pinellas County Government. That warning arrived before the two human dengue cases were confirmed, underscoring how vector control officials detected the elevated threat ahead of the diagnoses. The timing fits a pattern playing out statewide. Before Pinellas County's cases were confirmed, Florida health officials had already recorded at least three locally acquired dengue cases this summer in Hillsborough, Palm Beach, and Miami-Dade counties, according to WUSF. South Florida county health departments issued their own mosquito-borne illness alerts in early August, a trend Hoodline covered in its report on dengue alerts rattling Palm Beach and Miami-Dade. Why Rain Triggers a Mosquito Boom The biology behind the sudden spike traces back to the mosquitoes themselves. Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the primary vector for dengue, lay eggs that can remain dormant in dry soil or containers for up to eight months until rain triggers hatching, WUSF reported, citing expert research on the species. That means a single heavy rain event can awaken a season's worth of dormant eggs almost simultaneously, feeding the kind of population explosion seen in Hillsborough's trap counts. Infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit dengue through their bites, and unlike many native mosquito species that feed mostly at dusk or overnight, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes bite during daylight hours. That daytime activity means routine outdoor chores and errands carry real exposure risk, not just evening hours in the yard. Florida's Recurring Dengue Problem Pinellas County's cases land within a state that has repeatedly led the continental United States in dengue activity. Florida recorded 91 locally acquired cases across 10 counties in 2024, along with more than 1,000 travel-associated infections, with Miami-Dade County leading the state that year at 50 local cases, according to Outbreak News Today. In 2025, the state recorded 62 locally acquired cases, but the geography shifted: Brevard County accounted for more than half of them with 35 cases, while Miami-Dade recorded 25, marking the first time a Central Florida county led the state in local transmission. Pinellas County Mosquito Control monitors disease risk across all 24 local municipalities using 58 designated mosquito trap sites and eight sentinel chicken coops, which are tested weekly by state health labs, according to Pinellas County Government. The sentinel chickens serve as an early warning system, flagging when viruses begin circulating in wild bird populations before they spread more widely. That surveillance network sits alongside newer technology already deployed next door — in 2025, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management partnered with the University of South Florida to deploy AI-enabled smart traps and drone mapping aimed at identifying breeding hot spots like discarded tires, a program Hoodline detailed last year. What Dengue Looks Like and How to Avoid It Dengue is a viral illness, and symptoms typically develop within 15 days of an infected mosquito bite. Health authorities note the illness generally does not cause respiratory symptoms, but it can bring high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and sometimes a rash. Dengue does not spread directly from person to person — it requires an infected mosquito to bite and transmit the virus. Health authorities are urging residents to eliminate standing water around their homes, including in buckets, flowerpots, pool covers, and trash cans, since these are common breeding sites for Aedes aegypti. Officials also recommend fixing broken screens on doors and windows, wearing loose long-sleeved clothing outdoors, and applying EPA-registered insect repellents to skin and clothing. Residents who suspect dengue symptoms are advised to contact a healthcare provider. DOH-Pinellas maintains ongoing surveillance for vector-borne pathogens across Florida, which also includes tracking for West Nile virus, chikungunya, malaria, St. Louis encephalitis, and Eastern equine encephalitis. It remains unclear which specific neighborhoods within Pinellas County the two dengue cases originated from, whether the two patients are connected in any way, or which serotype of the dengue virus was identified — questions that remain open as investigators continue their work. Advertisement Lee County on alert as dengue season ramps up in Florida Mosquito season is underway, and with it comes the heightened risk of mosquito-borne diseases like dengue. Show more Show less 2:42 2:42 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save LEE COUNTY, Fla. (WINK)—Public health officials are testing mosquitoes in Lee County as the state continues to report new cases of dengue virus. Most people who get the virus don't develop symptoms, according to the World Health Organization. However, severe cases can be deadly. The Florida Department of Health reported 55 dengue cases across the state as of Aug. 1. The vast majority of those cases came from travel, the health department said. However, four cases were recorded locally. That means they came from mosquitoes in Florida, which health researchers said is rare. Hillsborough County reported two locally transmitted cases last week. Florida has dengue cases almost every year, said Professor Michael Teng, an infectious disease researcher at the University of South Florida. It's usually imported by people who travel overseas. "There are a lot of dengue virus endemic regions in the Caribbean and South America, so it's not uncommon to see in Florida," Teng said. "I think when we start seeing local transmission of the virus, then we start to worry a little bit because that's the way we can get an outbreak of the virus." Researchers are keeping an eye on the localized cases, Teng said, but they aren't a concern just yet. The only major Florida outbreak was between 2009 and 2010 on Key West, when 28 cases were reported. That doesn't stop local officials from keeping an eye out. "We literally are always on alert," said Jenifer McBride, communications director for the Lee County Mosquito Control District. When there is a confirmed or suspected case of dengue, the district will use specialized trucks to spray the neighborhood, McBride said. Lee County reported two cases of dengue so far this year, according to the Florida Department of Health. Both came from international travel. The district also said it proactively tests mosquitoes in a lab at its Buckingham headquarters. Mosquitoes are trapped and brought back to the lab for immediate results. The lab will grind up mosquitoes and run them through a test to see if they're carrying specific diseases. The district will often test Aedes aegypti mosquitoes - known as the backyard mosquito. That species can transmit other diseases, Teng said, including the chikungunya and Zika virus. "We rely on our community members really to make sure that they're dumping out the standing water in their backyard," McBride said. "That helps us tremendously."
