supplementary_news.content: August 13, 2026 1:55 AM हिंदी Home Latest National International Business Entertainment Science/Tech Sports Health/Medicine Video Subscribe Search Discover more Pest Control Travel Guides & Travelogues Geographic Reference Bangladesh dengue outbreak worsens, death toll rises to 59 as cases near 18,000 IANS August 8, 2026 11:23 AM Share on | Dhaka, Aug 8 (IANS) As Bangladesh grapples with a worsening dengue outbreak, at least 59 people have died from the disease, while 17,880 cases have been reported so far this year, local media reported citing data from the country's Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). History Discover more deaths South Asians & Diaspora Health Conditions According to DGHS data, Dhaka division has emerged as Bangladesh’s worst affected region, recording 6,871 cases this year, including 4,404 infections in Dhaka city alone. Infectious Diseases With 3,647 cases, Barishal division accounted for the second-highest number of infections, followed by Chattogram with 3,082 and Khulna with 2,272. Additionally, Dhaka division topped the list for dengue fatalities, with 26 deaths, 25 of which were reported in Dhaka city. Khulna recorded the second-highest death toll at 12, followed by Chattogram and Mymensingh with seven and six deaths, respectively, Bangladesh's leading newspaper The Daily Star reported. Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, has emerged as a serious public health concern in Bangladesh. It is primarily transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. GM Saifur Rahman, Associate Professor in the Department of Zoology at the National University of Bangladesh, said that the latest figure reflects Dhaka’s combination of high population density, persistent Aedes mosquito breeding, and inadequate vector control measures. The combination of high population density, warm climate and abundant breeding grounds reportedly provides ideal conditions for both Aedes mosquitoes and the dengue virus to circulate year-round, turning the Dhaka division into a major dengue hotspot. “Just a few days ago, while supervising an examination at Central Metropolitan Women’s College, I found Aedes mosquito larvae in a small container of water. Such breeding sites are common across the city, indicating that Aedes mosquitoes are reproducing continuously in residential areas,” The Daily Star quoted Saifur as saying. Stressing that the mosquito control measures have been largely reactive rather than preventive, he further said, “The most effective strategy would be to intensify mosquito control during periods when dengue transmission is relatively low. At that time, breeding sites are fewer, and interventions can be more effective. Instead, mosquito control usually intensifies only after the dengue season begins, by which time infections are already increasing rapidly.” Public Health According to Saifur, Bangladesh’s failure to establish an effective, centralised mosquito control mechanism has worsened the country’s dengue situation. He called for the formation of a national mosquito control authority staffed with expert entomologists to coordinate, monitor and oversee vector control measures nationwide. Discover more Death & Tragedy Insects & Entomology Biological Sciences “Until we establish a coordinated national control system, dengue cases are likely to continue rising,” he warned. Kabirul Bashar, Professor of the Zoology Department at Jahangirnagar University, warned that dengue infections are expected to surge through August and could continue their upward trajectory into September. “The peak may not occur in August. It’s possible that this year’s peak will come in September. What we can say is that the upward trend is likely to continue through August and into September,” he said. --IANS scor/rs LATEST NEWS Dakota Fanning says she, her sibling Elle panicked after learning they would share the screen in new film August 13, 2026 John Hinckley Jr. has a message for Jodie Foster 40 years after he attempted to assassinate US President Ronald Reagan August 13, 2026 APL 2026: Fifties by Nihar, Roshan power Tezpur Titans to first win of season August 12, 2026 Football: Sorloth's muscle injury a setback for Atletico Madrid August 12, 2026 Squash: Tanvi Khanna, Suraj Chand in semifinals of PSA Challenger Tour event in Kolkata August 12, 2026 Madhya Pradesh CM meets Gujarat counterpart during investment outreach August 12, 2026 135th Durand Cup: Indian Army FT seal QF berth with dramatic late win over Mohammedan SC August 12, 2026 India, Southern African Customs Union sign terms of reference towards trade pact August 12, 2026 Madhya Pradesh secures Rs 8,635 crore investment proposals from Gujarat August 12, 2026 Historic campaign for Indian origin quartet in PGA’s FedEx Cup play-offs August 12, 2026

supplementary_news.content: Image: Web New Delhi: Dengue cases are being reported earlier and continuing for longer in parts of India this year, prompting renewed interest in home remedies such as papaya leaf juice. However, doctors have cautioned that the drink should not be considered a cure or used as a substitute for medical treatment. Juice Papaya leaf juice has long been promoted as a traditional remedy for dengue, particularly for its perceived ability to support platelet levels. However, relying on it instead of appropriate medical monitoring can be risky, especially when the disease progresses or warning signs appear. Medical care remains important Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that can range from a mild illness to severe disease. Patients may experience high fever, headache, body pain, nausea and weakness, while severe dengue can involve bleeding, fluid loss and other serious complications. Doctors therefore advise patients with suspected or confirmed dengue to remain under appropriate medical supervision and follow prescribed treatment and monitoring. Platelet counts and other clinical indicators may need to be assessed depending on the patient’s condition. Home remedies should not delay treatment The growing popularity of papaya leaf juice highlights how quickly traditional remedies can spread during outbreaks. While some studies have investigated whether papaya leaf preparations may influence platelet counts, evidence is not sufficient to establish them as a cure for dengue. People should also avoid self-medicating and seek medical attention if symptoms worsen. Warning signs such as persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, bleeding, extreme weakness, breathing difficulty or unusual drowsiness require urgent medical evaluation. Health The key message for patients is simple: papaya leaf juice cannot replace professional dengue care . Early medical assessment, adequate hydration and careful monitoring remain important in managing the infection. supplementary_news.content: Virginia confirms first locally acquired dengue case - Virginia health officials confirm first locally acquired case of dengue virus, no evidence of continued transmission. (The Center Square) – Virginia health officials are monitoring for additional dengue cases after confirming the first documented infection acquired within the state. Officials say there is no evidence the mosquito-borne virus is continuing to spread. The Virginia Department of Health disclosed the case in a Tuesday letter to healthcare providers. The Northern Virginia resident had no known travel outside Virginia before becoming sick. Health officials believe they know how the infection happened. The resident had been in close proximity to another Virginian who contracted dengue while traveling internationally and was diagnosed a couple of weeks earlier. The Health Department said a local mosquito likely bit the person with the travel-related infection while that person was infectious and later transmitted the virus to the second resident. "There is no evidence of continued transmission and no additional reports of locally acquired dengue cases at this time," a statement from the Health Department said. "The potential risk for acquiring dengue virus in Virginia remains low." Still, state and local health officials are watching for additional cases. The Health Department is working with the Fairfax County and Loudoun County health departments to monitor for infections and mosquitoes capable of carrying the virus. Healthcare providers are also being asked to consider dengue when patients show symptoms consistent with the virus, even if they have not recently traveled. Dengue is spread primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. Symptoms can include fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and rash. Symptoms typically last two to seven days, and most people recover in about a week, according to the state Health Department. Severe illness is less common. The Health Department says about 1 in 20 people infected with dengue develop severe symptoms, which can include internal bleeding and shock. Most dengue cases reported in the continental United States involve people infected while traveling internationally, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Local transmission can happen because mosquitoes capable of carrying dengue are found in many parts of the country, but the CDC says the risk of widespread transmission remains low. Limited local spread has previously been reported in Florida, Hawaii, Texas, Arizona and California. Virginia health officials are urging residents to prevent mosquito bites and get rid of standing water around homes and businesses. Aedes mosquitoes can breed in water-filled containers as small as a bottle cap

CookDellUnited KingdomAcerMicrosoft WindowsMicrosoft 1 Sep 2026 Options When the rain comes, dengue season follows: 8 things to know Toggle article viewClose Tags.HealthDengue FeverMedicineInfectious DiseasesHealth ConditionsPhilippinesManila Doctors Hospital When the rain comes, dengue season follows: 8 things to know Daily Tribune (Philippines) 12 Aug 2026 FontsSaveListenSharePrintPage ViewMore +1Similar Stories The rainy season has arrived, bringing cooler mornings, cloudy skies, and muchneeded relief from months of scorching heat. But as the rain returns, so does a familiar health concern: dengue. Dengue, also known as “breakbone fever,” is a mosquito-borne viral infection transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. It can affect anyone, regardless of age or lifestyle, and may cause anything from flu-like symptoms to severe, potentially life-threatening complications. While dengue cases in the Philippines have declined, the disease remains a yearround public health concern, particularly during the rainy months. Here are eight things to know to help protect yourself and your family. 1. Dengue cases may be down, but the risk remains The Department of Health (DoH) reported 50,727 dengue cases from January to May 2026, a 56 percent decrease compared with the same period last year. The decline is encouraging, but dengue remains a public health concern. The rainy season can create more opportunities for Aedes mosquitoes to breed, keeping the risk present in communities. 2. Mosquito breeding grounds can be hiding in plain sight It does not take a flooded street or days of heavy rain for mosquitoes to multiply. Sometimes, the biggest culprits are hiding in plain sight: a small puddle in the backyard, an uncovered water container, a clogged drain, or a flowerpot that has collected rainwater. Regularly checking your surroundings and removing standing water can help reduce potential mosquito breeding sites. 3. Know the common symptoms of dengue Dengue symptoms typically appear four to 10 days after infection and can last for two to seven days. A sudden high fever may be accompanied by headache, pain behind the eyes, intense muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, rash and fatigue. Because these symptoms can initially resemble other common illnesses, it is important to monitor how symptoms develop and seek medical advice when necessary. 4. Know the warning signs of severe dengue Some symptoms may indicate that dengue is becoming severe and require immediate medical attention. These warning signs can include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, rapid breathing, respiratory distress, restlessness, excessive thirst, pale or cold skin, and extreme weakness or lethargy. These symptoms should never be brushed off, as they can signal severe dengue and potentially life-threatening complications. 5. Seek medical attention early When dengue is suspected, timely medical consultation matters. Rather than waiting for symptoms to become more serious, seeing a doctor early allows healthcare professionals to properly assess the condition, monitor for complications, and provide appropriate care. Manila Doctors Hospital can be a goto option for medical consultation and evaluation when dengue is suspected, particularly when fever persists or warning signs begin to appear. 6. Stay hydrated and be careful with medicines While seeking medical care, staying hydrated is important to help prevent dehydration. It is also best to avoid taking aspirin, ibuprofen, or other nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs unless specifically advised by a physician, as these may increase the risk of bleeding. Paracetamol is generally used for fever management, unless a doctor recommends otherwise. 7. Protect yourself from mosquito bites The Aedes mosquito is most active during the early morning and late afternoon, which means dengue prevention needs to happen beyond simply avoiding mosquitoes at night. Regularly check the home for standing water, keep water containers covered, change the water in vases, maintain clean surroundings, use mosquito repellent, wear protective clothing, and make sure window screens are intact. The DoH’s enhanced 4S strategy puts prevention into perspective: Search and destroy breeding sites, practice Self-protection measures, Seek early consultation, and Support fogging only during outbreaks as advised by health authorities. 8. Make dengue prevention a community effort Dengue prevention is not just about keeping one household safe. It is a community effort. Homes, schools, workplaces and public spaces can all become potential breeding grounds when standing water is left unchecked. The fewer breeding sites there are, the fewer opportunities mosquitoes have to spread the virus. So, as the rain continues to fall, remember that preparing for the season means more than keeping an umbrella by the door. Check what is collecting water around your home, stay alert to changes in your health, and do not wait too long before seeking professional advice. When it comes to dengue, prevention is always better than waiting for the fever to pass. And when symptoms appear, early consultation can make all the difference. supplementary_news.content: Thursday 13 August, 2026 Archive বাংলা HOME News PM President Top News National Arts & Entertainment July Uprising Education News Health News Climate Change & Environment Science & Technology Weather Business International District Interview Sports Notun Kuri Sports Subscriber NOTICE All News News Flash 16 years of accumulated problems cannot be solved in 5-6 months: Mahdi Amin Closer US business ties can boost Bangladesh economy: Kobir Humaiun seeks more job opportunities in Maldives Govt. won’t allow misinformation in statistics: Finance Minister All stakeholders must come together to deliver SDGs: Amir Khosru News BSS 09 Aug 2026, 14:28 Patients having fever advised to undergo blood test for dengue By Barun Kumar Das DHAKA, Aug 09, 2026 (BSS) - Specialist doctors have advised the people, who have been suffering from fever for one to two days to go to the nearest hospital for dengue test and seek medical attention if dengue infection is detected in the test. Talking to specialist doctors, it was learnt that the number of dengue patients is increasing across the country, including the capital. Among them, a significant proportion of the infected are children. This year, especially school-going children are being affected more with dengue. So, if anyone suffers from fever, he or she should get a blood test without any delay and seek medical advice as needed. In addition, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has also requested all to test their blood to detect dengue if they suffer from fever. Officials at DGHS said the government has made the NS-1 test for dengue completely free in all government hospitals in the country until December 31 and the CM test has been reduced from Taka 300 to Taka 50. According to the DGHS, 18,673 people have been hospitalised with dengue as of August 8 this year. Of them, 59 died. Of the patients infected with dengue, 61.5 percent are men and 38.5 percent are women. Some 10,827 are between the ages of 0 and 30, and 25 of them died. So far this year, 26 people have died in Dhaka Division. An analysis of the comparative report of dengue patients in 2025 and 2026 shows that 18,673 people have been infected with dengue as of August 8 this year, while the number was 23,410 in 2025. In 2026, 59 people have died from dengue so far, while in 2025, 95 people died from it during the same period. Both the infection and death rates are lower this year than that of previous year. Regarding dengue awareness, Dr Hasan Hafizur Rahman told BSS that the main way to prevent dengue is to destroy Aedes mosquitoes. “The first thing that is needed for this is to increase public awareness. So, we should all keep our house courtyards clean all times so that water does not accumulate under flower tubs, drums, buckets, air conditioners and refrigerators,” he said. The active participation of all in the destruction of Aedes mosquitoes is essential, he said. He said in dengue fever, the body temperature can rise to 102 to 105 degrees Fahrenheit. At this time, Dr Hasan said, the fever should be reduced by pouring water on the head and wiping the body. In addition, if the intensity of the fever increases, dengue tests should be conducted quickly, he said. DGHS’s Director (Hospitals) Dr Nurul Islam said even if the fever lasts for one or two days, dengue tests should be done as soon as possible. He also said instructions have been given to increase public awareness at the field level, and all hospitals in the country have been instructed to be ready due to the fear of an increase in dengue patients during the monsoon. “Necessary medicines and medical equipment are in stock. If the situation deteriorates, additional beds and separate dengue wards will be opened at hospitals,” he added.
